mcqs.question: An engineer argues the new `script-src 'nonce-…'` policy is the XSS fix, so the templates that print user comments can keep interpolating them unescaped. Their evidence: a stored payload that used an inline `<script>` stopped executing once the header shipped. What is wrong with that conclusion?
options: Nothing: the payload no longer runs, so the sink is neutralized and escaping the comments is redundant.
The payload was blocked, not the injection: the value still becomes markup, and the policy only covers one response.
CSP only covers reflected payloads, so a stored one should have been unaffected; the header cannot be the reason.
The nonce authorizes same-origin scripts only, so third-party scripts injected into comments still execute.
mcqs.explanation: Escaping at the sink is what stops untrusted data from becoming markup: the comment is written as text, in the context it occupies. The policy does something else — it decides which script tags the browser will execute in that one response — and the payload stopped because its `<script>` carried no nonce, not because the comment stopped being markup. OWASP keeps contextual output encoding as the primary XSS defense and CSP as an additional layer that limits a miss (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html), and the bank states the same ordering. So the injection survives: the same value rendered in an attribute, in a JSON document, in an email, or on a page served with a different policy is unprotected, because a policy is attached to a response, not to a sink. The strongest distractor is option 0 — "it stopped executing" is a fact about one payload's script tag, and reading it as "the bug is fixed" is how a heuristic control replaces the fix; a payload that knows the nonce is the case that team would still be left with. Option 2 contradicts the observation, since CSP is evaluated when the browser parses the response regardless of where the payload was stored, and option 3 confuses the nonce (which authorizes a tag) with an origin restriction, which `default-src 'self'` is doing.

mcqs.question: A user-supplied value is written into `href="…"` after HTML-encoding it. An attacker submits `javascript:alert(1)` and it runs when the link is clicked. What is the mistake?
options: Nothing: HTML-encoding the value neutralizes it, so the click cannot run anything.
Wrong context: `href` is a URL slot, so the value needs URL parsing plus a scheme allowlist.
Nothing: the code should have used `encodeURI`, the built-in function for encoding whole URLs.
The attribute quotes were not escaped, so the value broke out of `href` into markup.
mcqs.explanation: Encoding is per context, and this context is a URL, not HTML text: the parser decodes entities first and then hands the attribute value to the URL parser, so `javascript:alert(1)` arrives byte-identical — it contains none of the characters HTML-encoding rewrites — and the scheme is still `javascript:`. The fix is to resolve the value as a URL (`new URL(value, location.origin)`) and keep only `http:`/`https:` (or relative paths), then attribute-encode for the markup layer as a separate step. The strongest distractor is option 2 because it sounds like the canonical helper and it does leave the payload working: `encodeURI` does not escape `:`, so the scheme survives untouched (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/encodeURI). `encodeURIComponent` would percent-encode the colon and also turn every legitimate `https://…` into a relative path, which is an accident rather than a scheme policy. Option 3 is the right worry for an unquoted attribute, but this payload contains no quote to break out with, and option 0 is the single-encoder assumption the bank's source/sink model exists to break.

mcqs.question: A team sets `SameSite=Lax` on the session cookie and deletes the CSRF token checks, arguing the browser no longer attaches the cookie to a cross-site form post. Where does that reasoning break?
options: Nowhere: `Lax` withholds the cookie on cross-site POST, so a forged form can no longer authenticate as the victim.
`Lax` governs attachment, not authority: it still sends on top-level GETs, and a sibling subdomain is same-site.
`Lax` is honored only together with `Secure`, so without that attribute the cookie still travels on cross-site POSTs.
The break is browser support: clients that ignore `SameSite` still forge the POST, so the token only covers them.
mcqs.explanation: `SameSite` is a decision the sending browser makes about cookie attachment; it narrows which requests carry the cookie, and says nothing about whether the request came from your own page. So the forgery moves instead of disappearing. `Lax` still attaches the cookie on top-level cross-site GET navigations, which is exactly why no state change may live in GET. And `SameSite` is scoped to the site (scheme plus registrable domain), so an attacker page on a sibling subdomain is same-site and the cookie travels — the sibling-subdomain path the bank calls out. OWASP keeps a server-validated token on every state-changing endpoint and lists `SameSite`, `Origin` and `Sec-Fetch-Site` checks as defense in depth (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html). The strongest distractor is option 0: it is true about the narrow shape the team tested — `Lax` really does withhold the cookie on a cross-site form POST — so their repro passes and the argument feels confirmed, while the other reachable shapes stay open and the only control the server can verify itself is gone. Option 2 inverts the coupling (`SameSite=None` is the value that requires `Secure`, not `Lax`), and option 3 turns a structural gap into a legacy-support problem: the paths above work in current browsers.

mcqs.question: The session cookie is `SameSite=None; Secure`. A page at `https://evil.example` submits a form POST to `https://api.acme.test/transfer`, which answers with no CORS headers at all. What happened?
options: The browser refused to send it, because the response carried no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`.
The POST reached the server with the cookie and ran; only the response body was withheld from the evil page.
The server rejected it: a missing `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is a CORS failure the API enforces itself.
The browser sent a preflight first, and the missing headers stopped the POST at the `OPTIONS` request.
mcqs.explanation: CORS is the browser's read permission, not a gate on sending. The same-origin policy stops one origin's script from reading another origin's response, and the `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers are how a server grants that read. A form POST with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` is a simple request — no preflight, no custom headers — so nothing consults those headers before the request leaves, and the cookie rides along because it is explicitly cross-site (`SameSite=None; Secure`). The server therefore saw a valid session and executed the transfer; the only thing CORS changed is that `evil.example` cannot read the confirmation body. That is why the endpoint needs CSRF defenses and server-side authorization, and why "we never configured CORS, so nobody else can call it" is false (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS). The strongest distractor is option 2, because CORS is configured in server code and therefore sounds server-enforced: the headers are instructions to the browser, so a server that sends none has denied nothing, and a response with no matching grant is discarded by the browser after the request has already been processed. Option 0 mistakes a read restriction for a send restriction, and option 3 mistakes the preflight trigger: a simple form post has no preflight to fail.

mcqs.question: A credentialed fetch (credentials: 'include') is answered with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. What does the browser do?
options: Allows the response because both headers are present
Blocks the response: a wildcard allowed origin cannot be combined with credentialed requests
Downgrades the request to non-credentialed and retries
Sends an extra preflight to confirm with the server
mcqs.explanation: For credentialed requests the server must name one explicit allowed origin and allow credentials; `*` cannot be combined with credentials, so the browser refuses to expose the response. The first option is exactly the misconfiguration the rule exists to catch. There is no downgrade-and-retry behavior, and the constraint concerns response readability, not an additional preflight.

mcqs.question: Your organization uses an internal registry for `@corp/*` packages, but a developer's laptop falls back to the public npm registry when the VPN is down. Which supply-chain risk does the fallback create, and what is the control?
options: Typosquatting: a mistyped `@corp/…` name resolves publicly; the control is review of every dependency added to a diff.
Dependency confusion: a public `@corp/*` package wins resolution, so the build runs an attacker's code; the control is a fail-closed registry.
Install-script exposure: the fallback runs a stranger's `postinstall`; the control is installing with scripts disabled.
Lockfile drift: the fallback pins the public copy in the lockfile and CI then ships it; the control is a frozen lockfile.
mcqs.explanation: The resolver now has two places to look for one name, and the fallback means the private scope is not actually private: an attacker publishes the unclaimed `@corp/...` name publicly, and any build that cannot reach the internal registry installs that code. Because the delivery mechanism is a package, the payload is usually an install-time script, so it executes with the build's credentials before any application code runs. The control is to protect the scope and route retrieval through a registry that cannot silently fall back — internal proxy first, explicit failure when a private name is unavailable (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Software_Supply_Chain_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html). The strongest distractor is option 3: a frozen lockfile faithfully pins whatever was resolved, so if one public resolution lands in the lock, the attacker's version is exactly what CI keeps installing — it stabilizes the compromise instead of preventing it, and a newly added `@corp/…` dependency is not in the lock at all. Option 2 names the mechanism of harm but not the control for this path: disabling install scripts does not stop the wrong package being resolved and it breaks legitimate builds, so it is a mitigation, not a fix. Option 0 is a different attack — a typo in a name the developer actually meant — and a diff review cannot see a name that was already correct in `package.json`.

mcqs.question: A repository method now binds every value with `$1`, `$2` markers, but the sort column is still composed from a request parameter: `ORDER BY ${column}`. The team argues the query is safe because it is parameterized. What is the correct reading?
options: Safe: parameterized queries neutralize injection for the whole statement, so the interpolated column inherits the same protection as the bound values
Unsafe: placeholders bind values, not identifiers; the column must come from a fixed application-owned map with a default, because an interpolated identifier is still SQL syntax
Safe if the column is bound too, as `ORDER BY $3`, with the column name passed in the values array
Safe if the column is escaped with the driver's identifier-quoting helper and quotes are stripped from the input
mcqs.explanation: Parameter markers stand for data values: the statement's shape is already fixed, so an identifier cannot be a parameter, which is why the bank's rule is to map a user's structural choice onto an application-owned allow-list and fall back to a default for anything unknown (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html; https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-prepare.html). The strongest distractor is option 2: it is the natural extension of "bind everything", but the driver transmits the string as a value, so `ORDER BY $3` sorts by a constant — or fails type inference — and never becomes a column reference. Option 0 treats parameterization as statement-wide immunity, which is the misconception the identifier case exists to expose; option 3 replaces a reviewable policy with quoting, which may stop syntax injection but still lets a caller name a column they were never meant to sort by, and becomes injection again the moment someone concatenates that value elsewhere.

mcqs.question: A page must be embeddable only by `https://portal.example` and refused everywhere else. The team ships `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="frame-ancestors 'self' https://portal.example">` plus `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` from a shared template. What is wrong with this setup?
options: Nothing: the CSP directive and the legacy header complement each other and cover every browser
`frame-ancestors` is ignored when delivered in a `<meta>` element, so only `X-Frame-Options` applies — and `SAMEORIGIN` refuses the partner's cross-origin embed; both must be sent as response headers
It should use `frame-src` instead, because that directive lists the origins allowed to embed the page
It should add `X-Frame-Options: ALLOW-FROM https://portal.example` so the trusted partner is allowed to frame the page
mcqs.explanation: The requirement is enforced only by headers: CSP `frame-ancestors` is not applied from a `<meta>` element, so the policy actually in force is `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, which blocks the partner's different-origin frame and leaves the product broken while looking protected in source. The fix is to emit `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://portal.example` as a response header, keeping `X-Frame-Options` as the fallback for clients that do not read CSP (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/frame-ancestors; https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Clickjacking_Defense_Cheat_Sheet.html). The strongest distractor is option 2: it inverts the two directives — `frame-src` says what this page may embed, while `frame-ancestors` says who may embed this page — so following it would restrict the wrong direction and leave the page frameable by anyone. `ALLOW-FROM` is deprecated and not a working allow-list in current browsers, and option 0 is the naive "both mechanisms are present" reading that misses the meta delivery failure.

scenarios.prompt: A bug bounty reports two payloads against this route. `?name=` changes the tab title, while `?name=` does nothing at all. A `curl -i` of the same URL shows the CSP header byte-identical on every response. Explain what each result proves, name every defect, and fix the route so the reflection is inert and the policy still holds.
rubric: Names the raw interpolation of `req.query.name` into the HTML body as reflected XSS and puts context encoding at the sink as the fix, not input filtering.
Explains why the `onerror` payload dies under this exact policy: without `'unsafe-inline'`, inline event handlers are blocked, so that result says nothing about the injection being fixed.
Explains why the nonce-carrying payload works: a deploy-time constant is readable from any response's CSP header, so it is predictable rather than a secret.
Prescribes a per-response crypto-random nonce plus HTML-context escaping, and keeps the policy as the second layer rather than the fix.
Identifies what this policy still leaves open (for example no `base-uri` or `form-action`, and navigation that `default-src` does not restrict), and says CSP is per response, not per sink.

scenarios.prompt: A credentialed CORS review of staging produced two symptoms. (1) A researcher's page at `https://evil.example` read `GET /api/me` with the victim's tenant cookies attached (the session cookie is `SameSite=None; Secure`). (2) For the same URL, the CDN served a request whose `Origin` was `https://portal.globex.test` a response carrying `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.acme.test`, and the globex frontend could not read its own data. This middleware runs in front of every route. Explain each symptom, find every defect, and rewrite it.
rubric: Explains symptom 1 as arbitrary Origin reflection paired with `Allow-Credentials: true`: any origin that asks is told it may read, and `SameSite=None` is what lets the cookie travel so the read succeeds.
Replaces reflection with an exact allowlist match that returns that one origin, and notes that `null` and suffix matches must not pass.
Explains symptom 2 through the missing `Vary: Origin` on a shared cache, and adds it to the response as well as the preflight (appending, not overwriting).
Validates preflight methods and headers against fixed lists instead of mirroring `Access-Control-Request-Headers`, and fails the preflight closed for a non-matching origin.
States that CORS is a browser read policy, not authorization, and keeps tenant authorization plus CSRF or Origin/Fetch-Metadata checks server-side.

scenarios.prompt: This orders endpoint was written by a developer who 'already uses placeholders where it matters'. Find every injection hole, explain how each one is reachable, and rewrite the handler so the SQL structure is fixed and every user-supplied value travels as data.
rubric: Finds the concatenated `status` value, replaces it with a bound parameter, and explains why manual escaping is not an acceptable substitute.
Identifies `id IN (${...})` as the second value leak and fixes it by generating one placeholder per element while binding the array, not by joining coerced numbers into the SQL text.
Treats `direction` as a structural slot and constrains it with an application-owned map (with a default), instead of interpolating the request value or trying to bind an identifier.
Coerces and clamps `limit` to an integer (and preferably binds it), stating that type validation is a complement to parameterization, not the control.
Adds defense in depth — least-privilege database role and a regression test with a real payload — and notes that the allow-list for `sort` already present is the correct pattern to reuse.
